source.title: When Good Verifiers Go Bad: Self-Improving VLMs Can Regress on New Tasks

page_placements.theme: Self-improvement and self-labelling without a weaker supervisor

record.file_problem: The provided text contains the paper through its references and appendices; no truncation or garbling is apparent.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports verifier-guided self-DPO results in vision-language models, but it does not test the specified weak-model-supervisor/strong-student comparison or report PGR. Its verifier scores learner-generated candidates rather than providing labels as a weaker supervisor in the claim’s setup.
record.gate_note: The paper reports related results on verifier-guided preference training and transfer, but does not compare a student with a weak labeling model or measure PGR. The listed versions therefore are not tested. The rows below preserve the central accuracy results as related findings, not evidence for the specified weak-to-strong effect.
record.test_reason: The study trains small VLM learners (4B–8B) with self-DPO on their own candidates, ranked by frozen Gemini verifiers. The verifiers are far stronger than the learners, not weaker supervisors. No weak-supervisor accuracy, strong ceiling or PGR is reported. It neither tests nor uses the weak-to-strong finding. It touches the area only through scalable-oversight framing (cites Kenton et al.), not the original paper.
record.authors_conclusion: The record's paraphrase is accurate. The authors identify silent negative transfer: a verifier useful on one task (MathVista) can harm held-out performance on another (MMMU) while transductive gains persist. They argue that reliable updates need both gradient fidelity and transferability, and that MMMU is mainly transfer-limited. They present AAG as a mitigation of verifier-induced damage, not as a source of large gains.
record.recipe_differences: The study uses self-DPO on learner-generated candidate pairs ranked by a frozen evaluator, with AAG confidence gating as an intervention. It does not use the original weak-to-strong fine-tuning setup or calculate PGR.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported outcome varies by task and held-out versus transductive evaluation; AAG also varies with confidence threshold or retained coverage. The text reports only one seed for Qwen2.5-VL-7B and Qwen3-VL-8B in the main comparison, with multi-seed results for Qwen3-VL-4B.

fits_no_version.finding: On MMMU, raw verifier-guided self-DPO gains +3.52 points transductively on average but loses 1.42 points held out. AAG beats Raw held out in all six configurations (mean +0.98 vs frozen).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Verifier-scored preference training of VLMs can show silent negative transfer to held-out data; chosen-confidence gating mitigates it.

fits_no_version.finding: On MathVista (Qwen3-VL-4B/G3.1), raw self-DPO improves both transductive (+9.6) and held-out (+8.0) accuracy.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Whether verifier-guided VLM self-training transfers to held-out data depends on the task.

record.problems: The core weak-supervisor comparison and PGR are absent. Multi-seed experiments are limited to Qwen3-VL-4B; the larger learner runs use a single reported seed. The verifier APIs are closed-source and may change across versions. The authors note that their analysis is first-order and that AAG depends on confidence ranking remaining useful under distribution shift.
record.rows_left_out: Detailed chosen-response precision, reversal-rate, gradient-alignment, coverage, matched-budget, and preference-method ablation results are not included as rows because they do not measure the weak-to-strong supervisor comparison or PGR. They are reported in Tables 2–3 and 7–14 and Sections 5.3–5.6 and Appendices A.5–A.10.

untested.parts: There is no weak supervisor labelling for a stronger student, and no PGR. The verifier (Gemini) is stronger than the learner.
AAG is compared only with raw verifier-guided self-DPO, not on PGR in a weak-to-strong setup.
Learners and verifiers vary, but there is no supervisor-weaker-than-student comparison and no PGR scaling.
The held-out regressions concern transfer of verifier-guided self-training, not strong students exploiting a weak supervisor. Error similarity between weak and strong models is not measured.
The theory covers gradient fidelity and transferability and a Safe-Transfer Margin, not conditions for a student to beat its supervisor.
The models are vision-language, but there is no weak-to-strong setup and no PGR.

record.verdict_notes: All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The values match Table 1 and Table 6. The supervision direction is the opposite of weak-to-strong: a stronger frozen evaluator ranks a weaker learner's outputs. Relation 'discusses' is kept loosely. The paper does not cite or discuss Burns et al., so it is effectively T6 with only adjacent scalable-oversight framing. The ScienceQA replication (Table 10) and the ablations (Tables 2–3, 7–14) are also outside every version.

versions.untested_parts: No weak supervisor's task performance, strong-model ceiling, or PGR is reported.
AAG is compared with raw verifier-guided training, but the study does not measure PGR or the claim's weak-supervisor/strong-student effect.
The study varies learner, verifier and task, but does not measure PGR or compare supervisor and student sizes in the claimed setup.
The study reports held-out transfer regressions in verifier-guided VLM training, but does not measure PGR under distribution shift or whether weak and strong models err alike.
The paper gives theory for verifier-gradient fidelity and transferability, not conditions guaranteeing that a student beats its supervisor.
The study uses vision-language models but does not test the weak-to-strong effect outside language.
